items.statement:
Use the explicit unit crossing-ball foliation, with ordered saddle levels $h_1<\cdots<h_m$ in its middle band, and vertical projection $\pi(x,y,z)=(x,y)$. Let $N_i,S_i$ be the upper boundary arcs around the positive and negative $y$ directions, and let $E_j,W_j$ be the lower boundary arcs around the positive and negative $x$ directions.

The interior of $\pi(N_i)$ meets each of $\pi(E_j),\pi(W_j)$ exactly once if $j<i$, and not at all if $j>i$. At $j=i$ they meet only at their shared equatorial endpoint. All interior intersections are transverse. Along $\pi(N_i)$ from its northwest to its northeast corner the interior order is
$$W_{i-1},\ldots,W_1,E_1,\ldots,E_{i-1}.$$
The same order holds on $\pi(S_i)$ traversed from southwest to southeast, and reversing a traversal reverses the list.

More precisely, suppose these arcs belong to projected upper and lower intersection circles of a surface in the model saddle position. Let an upper circle $\gamma$ visit this ball only through $N_i$ or $S_i$, and let $D$ be one of its disk sides on the projection sphere. Push each common-face segment shared by the lower circles and $\gamma$ slightly to the outside of $D$, retaining their labelled lower saddle arcs and their connections, and make the finite corner adjustments transverse. If the projected overpass is in $D$, the crossing list on the chosen upper arc acquires the same-level arc at each end, namely
$$W_i,W_{i-1},\ldots,W_1,E_1,\ldots,E_{i-1},E_i.$$
If the overpass is outside $D$, the original interior list remains, with no same-level end crossings. No labelled lower arc meets $\gamma$ twice in this ball. In particular, if there are crossings, the one nearest either equatorial end is the same saddle's lower arc when the overpass is in $D$, and an arc of the next lower saddle when the overpass is outside $D$.

citations.quote:
Let $C=\{(x,y,z):x^2+y^2+z^2\le1\}$, with upper overpass $A_+=\{y=0,x^2+z^2=1,z\ge0\}$ and lower underpass $A_-=\{x=0,y^2+z^2=1,z\le0\}$. For every compact $K\subset C\setminus(A_+\cup A_-)$ there are $0<a<b<1$ and $0<\varepsilon<1/4$ such that, on a neighborhood of $C$, the smooth function
$$q(x,y,z)=\frac{z+x^2-y^2}{d(z)},\qquad d(z)=1+\sqrt{z^2+\varepsilon^2}-\varepsilon-z^2$$
has these properties:

1. $K\subset\{|q|<a\}$, $q\ge1$ on $A_+$ and $q\le-1$ on $A_-$.
2. For each $|h|\le b$, $D_h=C\cap q^{-1}(h)$ is a smooth proper disk transverse to $\partial C$. Projection to the $(x,y)$-plane identifies it with a smooth star-shaped disk. Its boundary meets $z=0$ in exactly four points, one in each open quadrant; its intersections with each open hemisphere are two arcs. The disks are disjoint and strictly ordered by height above every common projected point.
3. On $C\cap\{|q|\le b\}$ there is a smooth vector field $V$ tangent to the levels of $q$, with $(V_x,V_y)=(x,y)$, zero exactly on the vertical axis, and pointing strictly outward on $\partial C\cap\{|q|\le b\}$. Consequently radial dilation in these level coordinates is compatible with the boundary of the crossing ball.

This supplies the local foliation and vector field, not an ambient positioning theorem for a surface.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

derivations.claim: At a projected intersection of an upper arc of level $h_i$ and a lower arc of level $h_j$, the sphere heights are $z$ and $-z$ with $z>0$. Put $w=x^2-y^2$. Their equations in [F1] give $2z=(h_i-h_j)d(z)$ and $2w=(h_i+h_j)d(z)$. For $0\le z\le1$, $d-zd'=1+z^2+\varepsilon^2/\sqrt{z^2+\varepsilon^2}-\varepsilon\ge1-\varepsilon+z^2>0$. Consequently $R(z)=2z/d(z)$ is strictly increasing, with $R(0)=0$ and $R(1)=2/g(1)>2$. Hence a positive intersection is possible only for $h_j<h_i$, and then [F2] gives a unique $z\in(0,1)$ solving the first equation. The value of $w$ is uniquely fixed by the second.

These equations give an actual point in each quadrant. Let $b_0=\max(|h_i|,|h_j|)<1$ and $r^2=1-z^2$. The real identity $|h_i+h_j|/2=b_0-(h_i-h_j)/2$ gives $|w|/d=b_0-z/d$. But $r^2+z=1+z-z^2\ge d(z)$, so $r^2/d\ge1-z/d>b_0-z/d=|w|/d$. Thus $x^2=(r^2+w)/2$ and $y^2=(r^2-w)/2$ are positive. Their signs specify one point in each quadrant. It is on the northeast or northwest piece of $N_i$ when $y>0$, and on its east or west lower arc according to the sign of $x$. The same calculation covers $S_i$ with $y<0$. The intersections are transverse: in each open quadrant $(z,w)$ are local coordinates on the projected disk when $z>0$, and the Jacobian of the two level functions $(z+w)/d(z),(-z+w)/d(z)$ has determinant $2(d-zd')/d^3\ne0$. At $h_i=h_j$ the only solution has $z=0$ and is the appropriate corner; for $h_j>h_i$ there is none with $z>0$.

On the northwest quarter of $N_i$, increasing $z$ moves from the equatorial corner towards the positive $y$ axis. Indeed $x^2=(1-z^2+h_i d(z)-z)/2$ has derivative $(-2z-(1-h_i d'))/2<0$ by [F1]. The unique intersection height in step 1.1 increases when $h_j$ decreases, because $R$ is strictly increasing. The northwest crossings therefore occur in descending $j$ order from the corner to the axis; the northeast crossings occur in ascending order from the axis to the corner. This proves the displayed order. The negative-$y$ reflection preserves the level equations and gives the same order for $S_i$.

Only the same-level endpoint connections need adjustment when the common-face lower segments on $\gamma$ are pushed outside $D$. Their local behavior is explicit. Round the finite projected corners preserving their incident-arc order, and take a small chart in which $\gamma$ is the horizontal axis and $D$ is the upper side. The old shared common-face segment is on that axis. Push it to height $-\eta$. At a corner the same-level lower branch leaves the axis into the central, overpass side of the upper arc. If that is the $D$ side, join the pushed segment to this branch by a monotone transverse graph, giving exactly one crossing of the axis. If it is the other side, join them wholly below the axis, giving none. The fact that this branch is on the central side follows from its being the adjacent boundary arc of the same projected saddle disk, whose interior lies away from the corresponding underpass endpoint. These local graphs can be chosen in disjoint small corner charts and glued to small normal graph displacements along the finitely many common-face segments. They form explicit isotopies of the lower curve family, retaining every labelled lower arc and every connection.

Make these adjustments small enough to retain all transverse interior intersections in step 2.1 and introduce none elsewhere; compact separation from the other arcs and the finite local transverse charts permit a common positive size. The central-side case adds only $W_i$ at the first end and $E_i$ at the second; the other case adds none. Steps 2.1–3.1 show that every other labelled lower arc meets the chosen upper arc at most once, so the stated complete lists and nearest-end rules follow. As $\gamma$ has no other arc in this ball, they are also the complete crossing lists with $\gamma$ in this ball.

boundaries.reason: A chosen upper arc or a hypothetical nonempty word is required.

boundaries.evidence: Step 4.1 includes no lower intersections when the visit is noncentral and its saddle is the lowest.
Steps 3.2–4.1 include one level, adding only the same-level end crossings in the central case.

boundaries.reason: Ordered distinct saddle levels, embedded curves and transverse perturbations exclude degeneracy.

boundaries.evidence: Step 3.2 specifies the zero-or-one corner crossing while preserving labelled arc connections.
Step 1.1 has a unique scalar root under its finite inequalities.

risk_review.notes: Actual projected different-level crossings and exact shared-common-face perturbation are included. The word proof traces labelled lower arcs rather than treating projected saddle disks as disjoint.

constructive_supplier_evidence.exact_read_body:
1.1 Set $d_0(z)=1+|z|-z^2$ and $q_0=(z+x^2-y^2)/d_0(z)$ on $C$. Here $d_0\ge1$. For $z\ge0$, the largest numerator at fixed $z$ is $z+1-z^2=d_0$, with equality precisely at the points of $A_+$ at that height; the smallest numerator is $z-1+z^2\ge-d_0$, with equality only when $z=0$ and $x=0,y^2=1$. The corresponding inequalities for $z\le0$ follow by interchanging $x,y$ and replacing $z$ by $-z$. Thus $|q_0|\le1$ and equality occurs precisely on $A_+\cup A_-$. If $K$ is nonempty, let $m=\max_K|q_0|<1$ by [F1]; if $K$ is empty, put $m=0$. Choose $a=(1+m)/2$ and $b=(1+a)/2$. [given, F1, algebra, construct]

2.1 Write $g(z)=\sqrt{z^2+\varepsilon^2}-\varepsilon$. Since $0\le |z|-g(z)\le\varepsilon$, we have $d=d_0-(|z|-g)\ge1-\varepsilon$ on $[-1,1]$, and $|q-q_0|\le\varepsilon/(1-\varepsilon)$ on $C$. Choose $0<\varepsilon<1/4$ so small that this last bound is less than $a-m$ and $b(1+\varepsilon^2/2)<1$. Then $K\subset\{|q|<a\}$. On $A_+$ the numerator equals $d_0$, so $q\ge1$, and the negative counterpart gives $q\le-1$ on $A_-$. Positivity of $d$ also holds on a neighborhood of $[-1,1]$, where the displayed formula defines a smooth $q$. [step 1.1, algebra, choose, construct]

3.1 On $[0,1]$ we have $d'(z)=z/\sqrt{z^2+\varepsilon^2}-2z\le1$. This function is concave, since its second derivative is $-3\varepsilon^2z/(z^2+\varepsilon^2)^{5/2}\le0$, so its minimum is at an endpoint. The endpoint values are $0$ and $1/\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2}-2\ge-1-\varepsilon^2/2$, the latter inequality following by differentiating $(1+t)^{-1/2}-1+t/2$ for $t\ge0$. Since $d'$ is odd, $|d'|\le1+\varepsilon^2/2$ on $[-1,1]$. Therefore the level equation $F_h(x,y,z)=z+x^2-y^2-hd(z)=0$ has $\partial_zF_h=1-hd'(z)>0$ whenever $|h|\le b$. Each such level is a smooth graph on its projected domain by [F2], with at most one point above each projected point. At $x=y=0$ its equation has exactly one root in $(-1,1)$, because $d(1)=d(-1)=g(1)<1$, so the endpoint values have opposite signs. [step 2.1, F2, algebra, construct]

4.1 For $|z|<1$, put $H_h(z)=(z-hg(z))/(1-z^2)$. Its derivative has numerator $1+z^2-hA(z)$, where $A(z)=(1-z^2)g'(z)+2zg(z)$. For $0\le z\le1$, the definition gives $A\ge0$ and the identity $A=\frac{z}{\sqrt{z^2+\varepsilon^2}}(1+z^2)+2\varepsilon z\bigl(\frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{z^2+\varepsilon^2}}-1\bigr)$ gives $A\le1+z^2$. Oddness gives $|A(z)|\le1+z^2$ for negative $z$ as well. Hence $H_h'>0$. Also $H_h(z)\to\pm\infty$ as $z\to\pm1$, since $|hg(1)|<1$. Thus for every angle $\theta$ the equation $H_h(z)=h-\cos(2\theta)$ has a unique smooth root $z_\theta\in(-1,1)$. These are exactly the points of $D_h\cap\partial C$ with projected polar angle $\theta$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F2, algebra, construct]

5.1 The projected radial domain of $D_h$ contains the origin by step 3.1. On each projected ray its points form a closed subset of $[0,1]$; membership can change only at a sphere-boundary point, because every interior solution persists by [F2]. Step 4.1 gives exactly one sphere-boundary point on that ray, at the positive radius $r_\theta=\sqrt{1-z_\theta^2}$. Consequently that radial domain is exactly $0\le r\le r_\theta$. The boundary radius is smooth and positive, so this is a smooth star-shaped disk, and its graph is a proper smooth disk. For $h_2>h_1$, evaluating $F_{h_2}$ at a zero of $F_{h_1}$ gives $-(h_2-h_1)d<0$, so strict increase in $z$ places the second graph above the first wherever both are defined. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, F2, construct]

6.1 On the equator, the level equation becomes $x^2+y^2=1$ and $x^2-y^2=h$. Its four solutions satisfy $x^2=(1+h)/2$ and $y^2=(1-h)/2$, so all four lie in the open quadrants. Step 4.1 shows that $z_\theta$ has the sign of $h-\cos(2\theta)$: its defining increasing function has $H_h(0)=0$. It follows that the boundary has two positive-$z$ arcs around the $y$ directions and two negative-$z$ arcs around the $x$ directions. The four zeros are simple because $\sin(2\theta)\ne0$ there. [step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

6.2 Define $V=(x,y,-2(x^2-y^2)/(1-qd'))$ on a neighborhood of the closed level band; its denominator is positive by step 3.1 and compactness. Differentiating $F_h$ shows $dq(V)=0$, and $V$ is zero exactly when $x=y=0$. On the sphere boundary put $t=\cos(2\theta)$ and $r^2=1-z^2>0$. Then $V(x^2+y^2+z^2)=2r^2(1-hd'-2zt)/(1-hd')$. The boundary equation $t=h-H_h(z)$ gives $1-hd'-2zt=(1+z^2-hA(z))/(1-z^2)>0$ by step 4.1. Thus $V$ points strictly outward there; in particular the level disks meet the sphere transversely. [step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra, construct]

7.1 Steps 1.1–2.1 place $K$ in a middle level band avoiding both link arcs. Steps 3.1–6.1 give the smooth ordered quadrilateral disks, and step 6.2 gives the asserted level-tangent outward radial vector field. All parameter choices used finitely many strict real inequalities and all implicit solutions were unique, so no choice principle has been introduced. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 6.2] ∎
constructive_supplier_evidence.use: Actual q formula and derivative bounds are used in the projected-intersection calculation.

items.statement: Assume countable choice. Let $D$ be a connected alternating regular link diagram with at least one crossing, and let a closed embedded surface be transverse to the represented link and both shifted spheres. Suppose its crossing-ball pieces are finite ordered levels of the explicit quadrilateral saddle model and it is in bubble standard position. Then no cyclic bubble word has the form $P^iS^j$ with $i\ge0$ and $j>0$. Moreover every bubble word has at least two $P$'s. The assertion applies to both shifted spheres and does not require reducedness of the diagram.

citations.quote:
A **2-tangle diagram** is a regular diagram in a disk of two properly embedded tangle arcs and possibly finitely many closed tangle components, with four specified endpoints on the disk boundary; the arcs and circles are disjoint in the represented 3-ball, while their projections may have crossings. A **flyping circle** is a simple closed curve in the projection sphere whose intersection with the diagram consists of exactly three points, exactly one of which is a crossing; the circle is transverse to both branches at that crossing and to the diagram at the other two points. A small annular neighborhood of this circle has two complementary tangle disks. A **flype** fixes the tangle in one disk, interchanges which pair of strands crosses in the annular neighborhood, and turns over the tangle in the other disk: its projected tangle is reflected and all its over-under crossing data are reversed. This turnover is a half-turn in three-dimensional space about an axis in the projection sphere. Component orientations are transported by this motion, and the exterior diagram is fixed. The move with the opposite choice of fixed disk is also allowed; a disk containing no crossings is allowed. A flype whose fixed tangle has no crossings is called an **entire flype**. Diagrams are drawn on the oriented projection sphere; a **sphere planar isotopy** is an orientation-preserving smooth isotopy of that sphere carrying the decorated diagram. A plane diagram is obtained by choosing a point of the sphere outside the projection and deleting it. At each crossing of a link diagram, a **crossing ball** is a small 3-ball in which the overpass lies on the upper hemisphere and the underpass lies on the lower hemisphere, with the rest of the link outside that ball. Replacing all crossing disks by upper hemispheres or by lower hemispheres gives the shifted projection spheres $S_+$ and $S_-$. A **saddle disk** in a crossing ball is a properly embedded disk whose boundary meets each of the two hemispheres in two arcs and whose interior passes across the equatorial crossing disk. For a closed embedded surface transverse to the link and to $S_+$ and $S_-$, each component $C$ of its intersection with either shifted sphere has a **bubble word**: read once around $C$, recording $P$ each time it crosses the link and $S$ each time it passes through a crossing ball along a saddle disk. The surface is in **bubble standard position** if every such word is nonempty and no word records the same crossing ball more than once. A **Conway sphere** is an embedded sphere meeting the link transversely in four points; it is in crossing-ball standard position when its intersection with the crossing balls consists of saddle disks and its shifted-sphere intersection curves satisfy the bubble-standard conditions.

The turnover convention is the one in Kindred's Definition 2.9 and Figure 1. In particular, an entire flype permits viewing the whole diagram from the opposite side of the sphere, as in his Definition 2.11. Closed components inside a tangle disk are carried along with its arcs.

Let $D$ be a connected alternating regular link diagram with at least one crossing on an oriented projection sphere. Use crossing balls in the explicit quadrilateral saddle model and orient each shifted sphere by its projection to the given sphere. Let $C$ be an oriented simple circle on the upper shifted sphere, transverse to the link outside the crossing balls, meeting each upper hemisphere in at most one proper arc, each such arc being one of the upper boundary arcs of a model saddle. Record a cyclic word with $P$ for each link intersection and $S$ for each hemisphere arc.

For two successive bubble visits along $C$, with $k$ punctures between them, the two upper overpasses lie on opposite sides of $C$ if $k$ is even and on the same side if $k$ is odd. More exactly, if $\delta_i=1$ when the overpass in visit $i$ lies on the left side of $C$ and $\delta_i=0$ when it lies on the right, then
$$\delta_{i+1}=\delta_i+k+1\pmod2.$$
Successive visits are read cyclically, including a word with just one visit. Every such bubble word has even length. The same conclusions hold on the lower shifted sphere after exchanging upper and lower passes. Reducedness is not required.

Use the explicit unit crossing-ball foliation, with ordered saddle levels $h_1<\cdots<h_m$ in its middle band, and vertical projection $\pi(x,y,z)=(x,y)$. Let $N_i,S_i$ be the upper boundary arcs around the positive and negative $y$ directions, and let $E_j,W_j$ be the lower boundary arcs around the positive and negative $x$ directions.

The interior of $\pi(N_i)$ meets each of $\pi(E_j),\pi(W_j)$ exactly once if $j<i$, and not at all if $j>i$. At $j=i$ they meet only at their shared equatorial endpoint. All interior intersections are transverse. Along $\pi(N_i)$ from its northwest to its northeast corner the interior order is
$$W_{i-1},\ldots,W_1,E_1,\ldots,E_{i-1}.$$
The same order holds on $\pi(S_i)$ traversed from southwest to southeast, and reversing a traversal reverses the list.

More precisely, suppose these arcs belong to projected upper and lower intersection circles of a surface in the model saddle position. Let an upper circle $\gamma$ visit this ball only through $N_i$ or $S_i$, and let $D$ be one of its disk sides on the projection sphere. Push each common-face segment shared by the lower circles and $\gamma$ slightly to the outside of $D$, retaining their labelled lower saddle arcs and their connections, and make the finite corner adjustments transverse. If the projected overpass is in $D$, the crossing list on the chosen upper arc acquires the same-level arc at each end, namely
$$W_i,W_{i-1},\ldots,W_1,E_1,\ldots,E_{i-1},E_i.$$
If the overpass is outside $D$, the original interior list remains, with no same-level end crossings. No labelled lower arc meets $\gamma$ twice in this ball. In particular, if there are crossings, the one nearest either equatorial end is the same saddle's lower arc when the overpass is in $D$, and an arc of the next lower saddle when the overpass is outside $D$.

Supply a closed surface in finite crossing-ball saddle position whose disks are levels of the explicit quadrilateral model, transverse to the link and to the two shifted spheres, with compatible equatorial corner charts. Suppose a component of its upper intersection has a bubble word with exactly one $S$, and any number of $P$'s. Then some component of its lower intersection meets that same crossing ball in at least two arcs. The reflected statement also holds. Consequently a surface in bubble standard position has no bubble word of the form $P^iS$ for any $i\ge0$, without requiring alternation of the diagram.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

derivations.claim: Suppose an upper circle $C$ has the cyclic word $P^iS^j$ with $j>0$. If $j=1$, [F4] contradicts the lower no-repeat condition in [F1]. Hence assume $j\ge2$. The visited bubbles are distinct by [F1]. Project $C$ to the projection sphere and choose either of its disk sides $A$ using [F5]. All punctures are in the one common-face interval between the last and first saddle visits; choose a closed subinterval $I$ of that interval containing them. If $i=0$, choose any small nonempty subinterval there instead.

Project the lower intersection curves as well, and perform the small outside-$A$ perturbation of [F3]. It preserves their labelled arcs and all component connections, so a repeated label ball on a resulting curve is already a repeated ball on its original lower curve. All intersections with $C$ are now transverse and lie in the visited bubble disks; the common-face portions that originally agreed with $C$ are now outside $A$. Between the first two consecutive saddle visits there is no puncture, so [F2] puts their overpasses on opposite sides. Therefore at least one visited overpass is inside $A$, for either choice of $A$. At that visit [F3] gives two lower crossings of $C$. Thus the lower curves have a nonempty finite family of proper arc pieces in $A$, possibly together with closed circles contained there.

Choose a proper arc $\alpha$ in $A$ cutting off an outermost disk $A_0$ whose boundary interval $\beta\subset C$ avoids $I$. Such a choice exists with no other proper arc inside $A_0$. Indeed successive cuts along the finite disjoint proper arcs give disk regions by [F5]; their adjacency graph is a finite tree, since each additional cut splits one disk into two. It has at least two leaves. The connected interval $I$, which contains no lower crossing of $C$, belongs to only one region, so at most one leaf contains it; take a different leaf. Its boundary is one proper arc and one interval on $C$. Closed lower circles may lie in this disk but have no boundary endpoints and do not affect the choice. In particular the interior of $\beta$ has no lower crossing, and contains no puncture. Let $Q$ denote the one perturbed lower circle containing $\alpha$.

If the two endpoints of $\alpha$ lie in the same bubble, they lie on two different labelled lower arcs there: [F3] says one labelled arc cannot meet $C$ twice in that ball, and $C$ has only one upper arc in it. Both lower arcs belong to $Q$, so it repeats that bubble. By step 2.1 the original lower circle repeats as well, contradicting [F1].

Otherwise let $a,b$ be the distinct endpoint bubbles, ordered along $\beta$ from $a$ to $b$. Any complete intervening bubble visit has its overpass outside $A$: an inside visit would contribute its two same-level crossings by [F3], forbidden in the interior of $\beta$. Because $\beta$ has no puncture, [F2] alternates the inside/outside status at each successive visit. Thus there is at most one intervening visit. If none intervenes, exactly one endpoint visit is inside. If one, called $k$, intervenes, both endpoint visits are inside and the visit at $k$ is outside. At an endpoint of $\alpha$, the intersection is the nearest one to the corresponding equatorial end of its upper arc, since the remainder of that arc on $\beta$ has no further lower crossing. Hence [F3] applies with its exact nearest-end rule.

First suppose no bubble intervenes. If the inside endpoint is $a$, its endpoint arc of $Q$ is the same-saddle lower arc attached to the common-face path from $a$ to $b$. That unchanged path connects it to the same-saddle lower arc of the upper visit at $b$, so that latter arc also belongs to $Q$. But the actual endpoint of $\alpha$ at $b$ is an arc of the next lower saddle there, by the outside nearest-end rule in [F3]. These are two different labelled lower arcs in bubble $b$, both on $Q$, a contradiction. If the inside endpoint is $b$, reverse the tracing: the same common-face path instead gives two distinct labelled lower arcs in bubble $a$ on $Q$. This is again forbidden by [F1].

Finally suppose one bubble $k$ intervenes. Both endpoint arcs of $\alpha$ are the same-saddle lower arcs at $a,b$ by step 4.2. The common-face path from $a$ to $k$ connects the first to one lower arc of the saddle visited at $k$, while the path from $k$ to $b$ connects the second to the other lower arc of that same saddle. Both arcs at $k$ therefore belong to $Q$. They are distinct east and west lower arcs of one saddle, so $Q$ repeats bubble $k$, contrary to [F1]. All endpoint possibilities have now contradicted no-repeat. No upper word $P^iS^j$ with $j>0$ exists. Reflection gives the lower conclusion using the reflected assertions in [F2]–[F4].

A word with no saddle letters consists of a positive number of puncture letters by [F1]; its even length in [F2] makes that number at least two. A word with saddle letters and at most one puncture has cyclically the form $S^j$ or $PS^j$, excluded by steps 1.1–5.2. Thus every word has at least two punctures, as asserted.
